extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and formulating rejections under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including when to use a streamlined pathway, how to identify judicial exceptions, and how to assess whether additional claim elements integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant application / insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, printing/downloading, or routine physical activity) do not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information. For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim. Example rationale: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing the area of a space (a mathematical relationship) does not add a meaningful limitation to the process of computing the area. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitations do not alone confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception (i.e., merely linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment) do not amount to significantly more and cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Parker v. Flook; Bilski; Diamond v. Diehr) show that token or incidental field-of-use limitations (e.g., limiting a formula to petrochemical processes) are insufficient. Contrast: Diehr where specific limitations acted in concert to transform a product. Examples of such inadequate field-of-use/technological-environment limitations include (i) limiting drug administration to a patient population (Mayo), (ii) limiting hedging to commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), (iii) limiting a formula to wheel circumference (Flook), (iv) requiring execution in a computer environment (FairWarning), (v) limiting virus screening to telephone network/Internet (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), (vi) limiting collection/analysis/display to power-grid data (Electric Power Group), etc. Examiners should consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable for eligibility analysis and be aware of overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing generic computer functions in one environment does not add significantly more). See MPEP § 2106.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for efficiency when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo analysis and is not a way to avoid a proper ineligibility finding. If there is doubt about whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full Alice/Mayo analysis should be used. A claim that qualifies as eligible after Step 2A (Pathway B) or Step 2B (Pathway C) would also be eligible under the streamlined analysis. The record may simply lack an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks where Pathway A is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident (criteria for Pathway A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is suitable for streamlined review when, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception and its eligibility is self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes with meaningful limitations alongside a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using certain mathematical relationships); nature-based products that clearly do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; cellphone with an electrical contact made of gold). Close calls do not qualify for streamlined analysis and require full analysis. See MPEP § 2106.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to a technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that clearly improve a technology or computer functionality may be eligible without undergoing the full Alice/Mayo analysis because they are not directed to an abstract idea when appropriately claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Enfish; McRO) illustrate that claims directed to clear technological improvements can be treated as not abstract. When claims clearly improve computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, their eligibility may be self-evident and Pathway A or Pathway B may be appropriate. If the improvement is a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering example), perform the full analysis (Step 2B) to determine whether claims amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.06(b) and § 2106.05(a) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and support a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent, and a rejection should set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility with clear and specific reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples discuss substantive law but do not themselves form the basis for rejection. Examiners should review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law/prior art) before concluding eligibility. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06 and § 2106.07 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate each claim on a claim-by-claim basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should be evaluated separately for each claim because dependent or related claims may add limitations that change the eligibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is ineligible, dependent claims may be eligible if they add limitations integrating the judicial exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more. Conversely, dependent claims may be ineligible if they add only the judicial exception without meaningful additional limitations. Examiners must consider each claim on its own merits when forming rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: When a claim does not fall within a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is determined not to fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention, the rejection should explain why the claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.03 for discussion of Step 1 and the statutory categories. The Office action must provide an explanation sufficiently clear and specific to give applicant notice and enable effective response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter the limitations describe and why that described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as recited and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Identify additional elements and evaluate integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluation must explain that 1) there are no additional elements, or 2) the claim as a whole, looking at additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner concludes that certain claim elements recite well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. The rejection should explain for each part of the Step 2 analysis: identifying the exception, identifying additional elements (pointing to specific claim features), and explaining why those additional elements individually and in combination 1) do not integrate the exception into a practical application and 2) do not result in significantly more than the exception. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) and related subsections for required support and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, specific explanations in Office actions to enable applicant response
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, the Office action must provide a sufficiently clear and specific explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable to give applicant notice and enable an effective response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper rejection forms a prima facie case and allocates the burdens between examiner and applicant. When evaluating applicant responses, examiners must carefully consider all arguments and evidence; if applicant properly rebuts the examiner’s findings, the rejection should be withdrawn or rebutted in the next Office action. Under compact prosecution principles, examiners should also state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims (including 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting) in the first Office action.
